## Post 1 — hook  📎 fig2_soundness_by_method.png

We measured the "obvious" way to stop an AI from taking illegal actions —
block anything unreachable in the rulebook.

It barely helped. And when the model had bad habits, it did nothing at all
(4.3% vs 4.2%).

What DID work gets 100% valid output — guaranteed. 🧵

> **Alt text**: Bar chart titled "Only checking every step guarantees
> rule-following output." For a well-calibrated model: no enforcement 48.1%,
> reachability masking 61.5%, per-step rule check 100%. For a mis-calibrated
> model: 4.2%, 4.3%, and 100%. The per-step check is labeled "guaranteed by
> construction."

## Post 2 — the setup

The setup: give the AI a rulebook (an "ontology") — the kinds of things in a
domain, and the only legal steps between them.

In a shop: Customer fills Cart → Cart goes to Checkout → Checkout collects
Payment → Payment confirms Order.

Problem: language models freely generate steps that break the rules.

## Post 3 — the tempting fix  📎 fig1_reachable_vs_legal.png

The tempting fix: "mask the model's attention so it can't even look at
unreachable things."

The flaw: reachability answers *can you get there eventually?* — not *is
THIS step legal?*

Chess analogy: your rook can eventually reach almost any square. That
doesn't make every square a legal next move.

> **Alt text**: Diagram titled "A reachable destination is not a legal move."
> Boxes (Customer, Cart, Checkout, Payment, Order, Item) connected by solid
> arrows marked "each solid arrow = a legal step." A dashed red arrow jumps
> directly from Customer to Payment, labeled: Payment IS reachable via Cart
> and Checkout, so a reachability mask allows this step — but no rule permits
> it directly.

## Post 4 — the numbers

We generated 1,000 action sequences per condition and counted how many
contained zero illegal steps:

• No enforcement: 48% (good model) / 4% (bad model)
• Reachability masking: 61.5% / 4.3%
• Check every step against the rulebook: 100% / 100%

That last row isn't luck. It's enforced at generation time.

## Post 5 — loops make it worse  📎 fig3_cyclic_collapse.png

It gets worse. Real rulebooks have loops (Delivery goes back to Customer).

Add loops and *everything* becomes "reachable" — so the mask blocks nothing.
Its edge over doing-nothing collapses from +17 points to +1.

Per-step checks are immune. Topology doesn't touch them.

> **Alt text**: Slope chart titled "Add loops to the rulebook and reachability
> masking stops working." Between a loop-free rulebook (34.7% of pairs
> reachable) and a loopy one (100% reachable), reachability masking falls
> from 65% to 8% and no-enforcement falls from 48% to 7%, while the per-step
> rule check stays flat at 100%.

## Post 6 — it holds in the real layer  📎 fig4_attention_mass.png

Not a toy-model artifact. We audited our actual typed-attention layer:
two-thirds of attention mass lands on pairs that are reachable but are NOT
real rules. (And 0% leaks to unreachable pairs.)

The mask does its job perfectly. Its job just isn't soundness.

> **Alt text**: A single horizontal 100% stacked bar titled "Under a
> reachability mask, two-thirds of attention flows through non-rules."
> Segments: token attending to itself 16.9%, legal step (a real rule) 16.4%,
> reachable-but-not-a-rule 66.7%. Caption notes the mask blocks all
> unreachable pairs but admits 4× more pairs than the rulebook contains.

## Post 7 — the price of the guarantee

"Doesn't forcing rules ruin fluency?"

Only when the model disagrees with the rulebook — and you can measure that
disagreement exactly. Worst case in our tests: ~5.5 nats/sequence. When the
model knows the domain: ~free.

Bonus: the disagreement signal doubles as a live drift alarm.

## Post 8 — the receipt

The best part: because every step is checked, every output ships with a
receipt — a JSON certificate listing each step and the rule that allowed it.

Anyone can re-verify it with just the rulebook. No model weights. No API
access. No trust required.

Tampering? Detected. Rulebook drift? Detected.

## Post 9 — where this goes

Where we're taking this:

1. Auditable action & reasoning traces for frontier models — enforcement
lives at decoding time, so no from-scratch retraining.

2. Small models made provably reliable in a domain: the rulebook carries the
guarantee, so the model doesn't have to be huge.

## Post 10 — the honest caveat + links

The caveat we take seriously: "valid" means valid *under the rulebook*. The
guarantee is exactly as good as the ontology you wrote down. Wrong rules in,
certified-wrong behavior out. Writing good rulebooks is the real frontier.

Everything reproduces on a laptop:
github.com/MikeHLee/structure_of_clear_thinking
